translations.text: Saying of our holy father Basil concerning the Holy Spirit. He who is baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity is baptized by the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.
Not toward principalities, nor powers, nor other creatures; let it therefore be known to him
that the Trinity is above creatures, and let him not lower even one of the Trinity to the level of creatures.
For such is this theology of ours, and thus we preach: "He was the true light, who enlightens every man coming into the world": the Father;
"He was the true light, who enlightens every man coming into the world": the Son;
"He was the true light, who enlightens every man coming into the world": the Holy Spirit; and he was the Comforter.
And he was and will be, but thus he was light and light and light.
But this is one light, one God, which David understood beforehand and said: "In your light we have seen light."
And now we have seen and we preach the light from the light of the Father; we see the Son by that light of the Spirit.
This is the brief and good theology of the Trinity: let the denier deny, let the lawless act lawlessly. We, who have understood, preach.
Let us climb a high mountain and cry out, if those below do not listen to us; and we are not afraid to preach, but we are afraid to keep silent:
If there was ever a time when the Father was not, there was a time when the Son also was not; if there was ever a time when the Son was not, there was a time when the Holy Spirit also was not.
If one of these was always from the beginning, then all three were.
If you lower even one of these, I dare to say, do not exalt those two either;
for what is the profit of such a confession, that you do not confess perfect divinity? And, even more, what is divinity if it is not perfect?
And how would it be perfect if it did not have the Holy One? Or what Holy One would it have, except this Holy Spirit whom we preach?
Or let someone say whether there is anywhere a Holy One apart from this one. But if this is the Holy One, how is this one too not from the beginning, like the Son?
Or how would it be possible that God was ever without the Spirit, as those wretched and foul people say?
If he was not from the beginning, then he is counted together with me;
even if he were a little before me and is forever counted together with me, how would he make me god, or how does he unite me to God?
But remember how the Lord breathed the Holy Spirit upon the apostles and showed that the Holy Spirit is from the essence of the Godhead and not from the nature of creatures,
and again that saying of the apostle concerning the Trinity, in which we understand one power of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and one work,
of whom none is created and made by nature, neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit, for God does not do this, that he should distribute his own graces to all through a creature.
And the apostle says: "There are divisions of graces, and the same Spirit; and there are divisions of ministries, and the same Lord;
and there are divisions of powers, and the same God, who works all things in all."
Now therefore, whatever God does, the Holy Spirit does the same, for it says: "The one Spirit does all things and distributes to each individually as he wills."
Let no one dare to reduce the Spirit to servitude, for he does every work of God as he wills.
And again: "The Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom," for God's dwelling in us comes about through the Spirit, as John says:
"By this we know that he is with us, through the Spirit whom he has given us." For if the Spirit does not make God dwell in us, God is surely not with us.
And if God is not with us, neither life nor those eternal good things will be given to us.
Hear Paul, how he says: "Do you not know that you are temples of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?"
And again: "Your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God."
For created beings need revelation in order to know the things of God, and the Holy Spirit reveals them to us, as it is said:
"God revealed it through his Spirit, and he searches upon us," for it is through him that we carry out our searching, as it is said:
"The Spirit searches the depths of God," and he knows of himself, as our own spirit does, for it says:
"Who among men knows what belongs to a man, except that man's own spirit? So too, who knows what belongs to God, except the Spirit of God himself?"
And God gives life, for the Apostle says: "I charge you before God, who gives life to all," and Christ bestows life, who said:
"My sheep will hear my voice, and I will give them eternal life," and we are made alive by the Holy Spirit, for Paul says:
"He who raised Christ from the dead will give life to those mortal bodies of yours through his Spirit who dwells in you."
Now therefore it is clear that we are made alive by God through Christ, by the Holy Spirit. And for this reason, since every work of the Son is made manifest through the Spirit,
the Spirit too is called Lord, by the name of the Lord, and Christ, by the name of Christ, as we were saying just now: "The Lord is the Spirit," and again it is said:
"You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, for the Spirit of God is in you; but if anyone does not have the Spirit of God, he does not belong to Christ."
And then he went on to say: "If Christ is in you," in place of what he had been saying: "If the Holy Spirit is in you."
But there is no divine word that calls the Spirit created, for the saying that says:
"All things were made through him" was said with regard to the multitude of created beings.
But the Holy Spirit is not counted among the multitude; rather, together with those two he completes the Trinity, and he is outside created beings and far above them,
for he is the sanctifier and life-giver of created beings and the ointment of holiness, and he anointed even the body of the Lord himself with holiness.
But no one would ever dare to say this, that our Lord Jesus Christ was made holy by a created being, as the apostle Peter says:
"Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power." Nor is his power from a created being, for he says:
"By the Spirit of God I cast out demons." Nor was he led by a created being, for it is written:
"The Spirit led him up into the wilderness." But how could a created being have led him up?
And again, those first, ancient prophets used to say, "Thus says the Lord," whereas these new prophets said:
"Thus says the Holy Spirit," and the apostles used to say, "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us."
For this reason the apostle Paul too made it plain that he speaks from God, and at one time he said:
"If you seek proof of Christ, who speaks in me," and at another time he said, "I think that I have the Spirit of God."
And again, the old Scriptures too are full of the glorification of the Spirit, for the Psalmist says:
"By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power," and in the book of Job it is written: "It is the Holy Spirit who created me."
But just as it is not possible to conceive of another Word by which the heavens were established, other than the Son — for if they were created by another Word,

then surely they did not come into being through the Lord Jesus — so too it is not possible to conceive of another Spirit who together with that Word establishes the powers of heaven, except this Holy Spirit.
But when we hear of the Spirit of the mouth, let us not understand it in a human way, but as befits God.
For just as the Word is not a word of the kind that scatters into the air, but as the Psalm says, "Forever, O Lord, your word stands firm in the heavens,"
so too the Spirit is not some breath that dissipates into the air, but is firm and unshakable, for it has been said:
"Where shall I go from your Spirit, or where shall I flee from your face?"
For that Spirit is holy and has filled all things, and has the honor of divinity.
For what he said about the Spirit, the same he says about the face of God and about his right hand: "Where shall I flee from your face?
If I go up to heaven, you are there; if I go down to hell, there too you are near.
If I lift up my hands at dawn and settle at the end of the sea, even there your hand will lead me and your right hand will receive me."
And again the voice of the Lord speaks about himself and about the Holy Spirit: "I am among you, says the Lord, and my Spirit shall abide upon you."
Therefore the Holy Spirit is not foreign to the glory of God, but proceeds ineffably from that ineffable mouth; nor is he confused with the Father and the Son,
but he is the Spirit of God and is with God, and he is sent from God and given to us through the Son, as is said from the mouth of the Father:
"My Spirit, which is upon you," and again it is said by the Lord: "I will send you another Comforter," whom he also calls the Spirit of truth.
Therefore, according to the teaching of the saints, one must confess one Father and one Son and one Holy Spirit, and not two fathers nor two sons, for the Spirit is not a son, nor is he called a son.
For we do not receive anything from the Spirit in the way that we receive the Spirit from the Son.

Rather, the Holy Spirit himself comes to sanctify us, and we receive him as participation in divinity, as giver of sonship, as a pledge of those eternal inheritances, and as the beginning of those unending good things.
And let no one search out anything beyond these holy names; let them not strive to apply the name of Son to the Holy Spirit, nor birth, but let the name of Spirit and the likeness be enough for them.

I, then, believe this in this way, and may whoever is my friend also believe in this way, so that you may believe in God the Father and God the Son and God the Holy Spirit: three properties and one divinity,
undivided in glory and honor and kingship and essence, as those other God-clothed men have preached.
And whoever does not believe in this way, let him not see the morning star rising, as Scripture says: "Nor let him see the glory of the radiance to come,"
whoever does not hold it in this way, or follows along with the times and changes to one thing and another, and reasons wickedly about these great matters.
For if the Holy Spirit is not to be worshipped, how does he make me God through baptism?
And if he is to be worshipped, how is he not worthy of honor? And if he is worthy of honor, how is he not God?

One link is joined to another of this truly golden and life-giving chain: through the Spirit second birth is given to us, and from second birth renewal, and from renewal knowledge of the honor of our Renewer.
And again, let those whose eyes of the soul have not been completely closed [?] consider the multitude of his works, through which his divinity is truly understood.
For consider it in this way: Christ was born, and he ran before him; he was baptized, and he bore witness to him;
he was tempted, and he led him up into the wilderness; he worked mighty deeds, and he was with him; Christ ascended, and he appeared.
For what is there among these great works that he who is God cannot do?
Or what divine name is he not called, apart from unbegottenness and begottenness?
For it was fitting that those properties should remain those of the Father and the Son, so that there should be no confusion in God, who bestows order on others.
But I tremble when I call to mind the multitude of his names, and against how many of them those who oppose the Holy Spirit have been blinded.
For he is called the Spirit of God, the Spirit of Christ, the Spirit of the Lord, the Lord himself, "the Spirit of adoption, of truth,
of freedom, the Spirit of wisdom, of knowledge, of counsel, of might, of understanding, of reverence, of the fear of God.
For he is the doer of all these things, the filler of all things, the holder of all things, uncontainable in the world by his power, good, upright,
sovereign by nature, sanctifying and not by gift, not sanctified by anyone else, reckoning and not reckoned, filling and not filled,
holding and not held, granting inheritance, glorified, counted together with the Father and the Son, the finger of God, fire, God, creating Spirit,
renewer through baptism and resurrection; the Spirit who knows all things, teacher, who goes wherever he wills and as much as he wills, guide,
speaker, sender, one who sets apart, one who is angered at the lawless, revealer, enlightener, life-giver, and rather himself light and life;
maker of temples, maker of gods, perfecter, who comes before baptism and is sought after baptism, worker of every divine deed,
divider of the tongues of fire, distributor of graces, enlightener of apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds, and teachers;
intelligible, manifold, dividing, immeasurable, great, unhindered, undefiled, all-wise, manifold in his working and revealer of all things, self-governing,
unchangeable, all-powerful, overseer of all, spreading over all spirits, those intelligible, pure, and subtle angelic powers,
and likewise those of prophets and apostles, at the same time and not in one place, but when one is in one place and another in another,
and he spreads over all, by which his uncircumscribability is shown; and, above all, Comforter.
For thus they spoke and thus they taught us, those holy preachers, who call him God, and who know that blasphemy against him alone is unforgivable,
by whom Ananias and Sapphira were so terribly exposed, because he lied to the Holy Spirit and not to a man.
What do you say, O speaker of vanity? Did they not preach him to us as God?
How hard you are and how far from that Holy Spirit, if you do not understand this but need a teacher!
These are his names, and so good they are. But as for however many lowly words are spoken concerning him [?], that is:
giving, sending, dividing, bestowing, breathing-in, promise, prayer, and everything similar to these, so that I may not speak of each one individually,
understand all of it as referring to that first Cause, so that his being from that power may be shown, and so that we may not introduce three principalities divided from one another.
For merging in the Sabellian way and dividing in the Arian way are equal in lawlessness;
the one in hypostasis and the other in nature. This I have examined at length within myself with the earnestness of my mind, and I have turned my reasoning in every direction,
and I have gone over many things and searched, so that I might find some image of such a matter, and I found nothing that could be an image of that nature of the Godhead.
For even if some small likeness is found, the greater part escapes, and I am left below with the image.

I thought of an eye, a spring, and a river, and others have also thought of this, whether perhaps the one might serve as an image of the Father, the second of the Son, and the third of the Holy Spirit.
For these are neither separated from one another in time, nor is one cut off from the other, and they are reckoned as though divided by three properties.
But I trembled, first for this reason, lest I introduce flowing and instability into that holy nature, and again for this reason,
lest by this image oneness of hypostasis be introduced, for eye, spring, and river are one in hypostasis, and they are distinguished in various forms.
Again I thought of the sun, a ray, and light, but here too I was afraid, first for this reason, lest some compositeness be introduced into that uncompounded nature,
as the sun and its works are; and secondly for this reason: lest perhaps we make the Father a person and not the others,
but speak of them as a power of God joined to him and not as persons. For neither the radiance nor the light are other suns, but they are things that go forth from the sun, and its powers.
And so, on the basis of this image of ours, we would ascribe to God both being and non-being, which is impiety.
And so there is nothing at all that has been able to convince my mind, but in everything an objection is found.
Unless someone were to proceed in this way: to take some one thing from the image and leave the rest. But as for me, in the end I have been pleased with this:
to withdraw from the search for images, as things that are deceptive and unable to find the truth.
And I shall hold to good thought and use the Holy Spirit as my guide, so that in this way the radiance
that has shone upon me here I may keep to the end by his power, and that he, as a good counselor,
may lead me well through this present world, and that I may also preach to all others to worship the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit,
the one Godhead and the one power; for to him belongs all glory and honor and might, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
